idiom_name: MapStruct @Mapper interface generating a plain-Java implementation at build time
implementation_notes: The mainstream Java answer is MapStruct: declare `@Mapper` on an interface with `UserDto toDto(User u)` and `User fromDto(UserDto d)`, and the annotation processor generates a plain-Java implementation at build time, so the invocation is `UserMapper.INSTANCE.toDto(user)` or an injected Spring bean. Individual fields get `@Mapping(source = ..., target = ...)`, and because the implementation is generated and compiled, a renamed property fails the build instead of silently dropping data - the property that makes it preferable to runtime reflection mappers. Keep the domain type free of annotations: the mapper interface lives in the boundary layer and only it knows both shapes.
pitfalls: Generated implementations are invisible in review: a missing `@Mapping` on a same-named property maps by convention, so correctness still needs tests.
The annotation processor runs in every module that declares a mapper; a mis-scoped dependency silently turns the mapper into a `null` INSTANCE at runtime.
Mapping interfaces drift into the domain package when they are seen as 'just interfaces'; keep them in the boundary module so the domain does not depend on the wire shape.

variants.name: Hand-written mapper class over records
variants.idiom_name: hand-written mapper class or static factory methods (records make it a constructor call)
variants.implementation_notes: For a stable pair of shapes, a hand-written mapper class - `public UserDto toDto(User u)` plus `public User fromDto(UserDto d)` - is honest and dependency-free, and records turn it into plain constructor calls (`new User(u.id(), u.fullName())`). Keep both directions in one class per pair, inject it as a bean only when it needs collaborators, and model absent values explicitly (`Optional`, `@Nullable`, or a field on the DTO) instead of letting null default silently. Choose this when mapping rules are few, when the shapes are tightly coupled, or when the build must not carry an annotation processor; records also make the target immutable, so a future field addition shows up as an uncompilable constructor call rather than a dropped value.
pitfalls: Runtime reflection mappers (ModelMapper, Dozer) discover mismatches only in production; MapStruct's compile-time generation exists to avoid exactly that.
Records are shallowly immutable: lists and nested objects passed into them stay shared, so mutating the source afterwards mutates the mapped value unless you copy.
Nulls in the source pass straight through unless the mapper states a policy; an absent field and an explicitly null field end up indistinguishable downstream.
